Estrange

ih-STRAYNJ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To estrange is to isolate someone from a close relationship.

Years of unreturned phone calls slowly began to estrange the two sisters from one another.

Worked Example

A bitter argument over their father's will estranged the brothers for nearly a decade.

Estrange describes the slow or sudden breakdown of closeness between people who were once family or close friends, usually leaving them living separate, distant lives.

How Estrange Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

alienate

alienate: cause someone to feel isolated or distant

distance

distance: make someone feel less close

Antonyms

reconcile

reconcile: restore a friendly relationship

reunite

reunite: bring back together

How Strong Is It? — annoy → estrange → disown

annoy vs. estrange

annoy vs. estrange: Annoying someone is a brief, minor friction; it rarely breaks a relationship on its own.

disown vs. estrange

disown vs. estrange: To disown someone is to formally reject them as family, a far more permanent and total break than simply becoming estranged.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of estrange.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e-

prefix — e-: out (Latin (ex-))

root — strange

root — strange: foreign, external (Old French (estrange, from Latin extraneus))

Put it together

Put it together: e- ("out") + strange ("foreign") = to make someone feel like an outsider to a relationship.

Use the root in a new word: extraneous

Use the root in a new word: extraneous: The same Latin root, extraneus, also gives us "extraneous," meaning off-topic or coming from outside -- you already met this word earlier in this course. Both words share the idea of something pushed to the outside.

Root Check

Word Choice

Estrange describes the breakdown of a personal relationship -- family or close friends -- rather than a whole group's decision to exclude someone, which is closer to what Ostracize describes.
